title: Mumbai’s Eleftheria Konark Named Best Indian Cheese at World Cheese Awards 2026
excerpt: The Bhandup-made chariot-wheel cheese led a four-award haul for India in Córdoba, seven months after Prime Minister Modi praised the same brand for its Brazil medals.
body:
• Eleftheria Konark, made in Bhandup, Mumbai, by Vivanda Gourmet, has been named Best Indian Cheese at the World Cheese Awards 2026 in Córdoba, Spain.
  • India took home four awards in total — one Gold, two Silver and one Bronze — from a field of 5,330 entries from 45 countries, judged blind by 270 experts.
  • Konark is a semi-hard, washed-curd cow’s milk cheese, matured for three months and shaped like the chariot wheel of Odisha’s Konark Sun Temple.
  • The win comes seven months after Prime Minister Narendra Modi publicly praised the same Mumbai brand’s medal haul at a cheese championship in Brazil.

A cheese made in Bhandup West, Mumbai, has been named the best Indian cheese in the world’s largest cheese competition. Eleftheria Konark, produced by Vivanda Gourmet, took the Best Indian Cheese trophy at the World Cheese Awards 2026, held at the Centro de Exposiciones, Ferias y Convenciones de Córdoba in Spain, with judging on Thursday, November 12, and results announced on November 16 by the Guild of Fine Food, which organises the awards.

The winning cheese

Konark is a semi-hard, pasteurised cow’s milk cheese made with vegetarian rennet and matured for three months. A washed-curd cheese, it is shaped to resemble an ancient chariot wheel — a reference to the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha, whose stone wheels give the cheese its name and form. It is not a newcomer to this stage: Konark previously won Gold at the World Cheese Awards 2023 in Norway and Silver at the 2025 edition in Switzerland.

India’s wider haul at Córdoba ran to four awards — one Gold, two Silver and one Bronze — including a Silver for Eleftheria Drama Queen, also from Vivanda Gourmet.

How the awards work

The 2026 edition, the 38th World Cheese Awards, drew 5,330 entries from 45 countries, assessed by 270 judges from 51 countries. Judging is entirely blind: packaging and identifying marks are removed, and teams of two or three score each cheese on the appearance of its rind and paste, its aroma, body and texture, with most points awarded for flavour and mouthfeel. The top cheeses are then re-assessed by a 14-member Super Jury, which chose the World Champion Cheese live: Comté PDO Fort des Rousses, aged 24 months, from Fromageries Arnaud in France, according to the Guild of Fine Food’s results announcement.

“Cheese from India makes its mark globally… Congratulations to Mausam Narang and Thenlay Nurboo.”

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on X, April 22, 2026

A brand the Prime Minister noticed

Eleftheria, founded in Mumbai by Mausam Narang, who left a corporate career at Capgemini to make cheese, had already had a remarkable 2026. At India’s debut at the Mundial do Queijo do Brasil in São Paulo in April, its Gulmarg, a Brie-style cheese, won Super Gold, its Brunost whey cheese won Gold and its Kaali Miri won Silver, while Nordic Farm’s Yak Churpi-Soft from Leh, Ladakh, also took Gold. Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated the makers on X on April 22 and returned to the wins in his Mann Ki Baat address on April 26. Eleftheria works with four family-run farms across Maharashtra, using cow and goat milk.

What it signals

India’s cheese tradition has long meant paneer at home and imported brands for everything else. A Mumbai-made, French-style tomme taking a country trophy at the World Cheese Awards — in blind judging against 5,330 entries, most of them European — is evidence that the country’s small artisanal makers can now compete on flavour alone, with no origin story doing the work for them. For Narang’s Eleftheria, the Córdoba trophy completes a year in which the same creamery collected medals on two continents.
